To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the basic protein of the myelin sheath is cross-reactive with cancer tissue.
the basic proteins of myelins from human, bovine, and rat brains and the basic protein common to human cancer tissue are immunologically cross-reactive in man and in guinea-pig.
basic protein of human cancer tissue is immunologically cross-reactive in guinea-pig lymphocytes to basic protein of myelinated nerve fibres.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the immunological cross-reactivities between myelin basic protein and a basic protein found in human cancer tissues, and with the possible implications of this cross-reactivity in the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis and in immunotherapy for human cancer.
the possibility of immunological cross-reactivities between basic proteins of the nervous system and those of cancer.
the question of immunological cross-reactivities between basic proteins of the myelin sheath and of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immunological cross-reactivities between basic proteins of cancer and of myelin are real and are not due to the presence of other proteins.
the immunological cross-reacting basic protein of human cancer tissue is a basic protein of human nervous tissue.
there is no evidence of cross-reactivity in man between basic proteins of cancer tissue and myelin basic protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the basic protein of myelinated nerve fibres, and a basic protein of human cancer tissue, have a number of common antigenic determinants.
basic protein of myelinated nerve is antigenically cross-reactive with a basic protein of cancer.
basic proteins of myelinated nerve and basic proteins of cancer tissue are antigenically similar in guinea-pig, rat, rabbit, mouse, dog, and man.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that the immune system of guinea pigs can be sensitized against both myelin and tumor antigens and that these sensitized lymphocytes can be used to detect the presence of the antigen.
the immune system can recognize cancer cells as “non-self” and can mount an immune attack.
the immune system is not a simple system, and that the immune system can respond in different ways to the same stimulus.
